prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper deals with the investigation of the solution of an unified fractional reaction-diffusion equation associated with the Caputo derivative as the time-derivative and Riesz-Feller fractional derivative as the space-derivative. The solution is derived by the application of the Laplace and Fourier transforms in closed form in terms of the H-function. The results derived are of general nature and include the results investigated earlier by many authors, notably by Mainardi et al. (2001, 2005) for the fundamental solution of the space-time fractional diffusion equation, and Saxena et al. (2006a, b) for fractional reaction- diffusion equations. The advantage of using Riesz-Feller derivative lies in the fact that the solution of the fractional reaction-diffusion equation containing this derivative includes the fundamental solution for space-time fractional diffusion, which itself is a generalization of neutral fractional diffusion, space-fractional diffusion, and time-fractional diffusion. These specialized types of diffusion can be interpreted as spatial probability density functions evolving in time and are expressible in terms of the H-functions in compact form.

outputs.L3:
The paper investigates a unified fractional reaction–diffusion equation formulated in terms of the Caputo fractional derivative in time and the Riesz–Feller fractional derivative in space. This framework captures both temporal memory effects and nonlocal, potentially asymmetric spatial transport, making it suitable for modeling a broad range of anomalous diffusion and reaction processes.

The equation is solved by applying the Laplace transform to the time variable and the Fourier transform to the spatial variable. After solving the transformed equation and performing the corresponding inverse transforms, the solution is obtained in closed form in terms of the Fox H-function. This representation provides a compact and flexible way to describe the resulting solution kernels and their dependence on the fractional parameters.

The general solution includes, as special or limiting cases, several earlier results for space–time fractional diffusion and fractional reaction–diffusion equations. In particular, the use of the Riesz–Feller space derivative naturally incorporates the fundamental solution of the space–time fractional diffusion equation. This fundamental solution unifies several important models, including neutral fractional diffusion, space-fractional diffusion, and time-fractional diffusion.

These specialized diffusion processes admit a probabilistic interpretation: their fundamental solutions can be viewed as spatial probability density functions that evolve over time. Expressing these densities through H-functions yields a concise representation while also making the relationships among the different fractional diffusion models transparent.
outputs.L4:
The paper develops a unified analytical treatment of a broad class of fractional reaction–diffusion equations involving both temporal and spatial nonlocality. The model combines a Caputo fractional derivative in time with a Riesz–Feller fractional derivative in space and may also include a reaction or source term. Because the Caputo derivative allows the use of conventional initial conditions, while the Riesz–Feller operator incorporates both anomalous spatial scaling and directional asymmetry, the resulting equation provides a flexible framework for describing anomalous transport, diffusion, and reaction processes.

A closed-form solution is derived by applying the Laplace transform with respect to time and the Fourier transform with respect to the spatial variable. In transform space, the fractional differential equation reduces to an algebraic expression involving the characteristic symbol of the Riesz–Feller operator. The inverse Laplace transform introduces Mittag–Leffler functions, and the subsequent inverse Fourier transform yields the fundamental solution. This solution is expressed compactly in terms of the Fox \(H\)-function, whose general structure makes it particularly suitable for representing the probability densities associated with fractional evolution equations.

The resulting formula describes the time-dependent spatial density generated by a localized initial condition and can also be extended to more general initial data and source terms through convolution. The parameters controlling the orders of the time and space derivatives determine the scaling, spreading rate, and asymmetry of the density. The time-fractional order accounts for memory effects and anomalously slow or fast temporal evolution, whereas the order and skewness parameter of the Riesz–Feller derivative govern the heavy-tailed and potentially asymmetric character of spatial transport.

An important feature of the analysis is that many established diffusion models appear as special or limiting cases of the unified solution. Appropriate parameter choices recover the space–time fractional diffusion equation, the neutral fractional diffusion equation, purely space-fractional diffusion, and purely time-fractional diffusion. The classical diffusion kernel is obtained when both fractional derivative orders reduce to their standard integer values and the spatial operator becomes the ordinary symmetric Laplacian. Symmetric parameter choices also recover Lévy-stable densities, while more general choices describe skewed stable distributions and non-Markovian transport.

The \(H\)-function representation brings these different results into a single mathematical form, clarifying their relationships and avoiding the need to derive each case separately. It also provides a useful basis for studying normalization, positivity, scaling behavior, asymptotic decay, and fractional moments of the evolving densities. By unifying earlier formulas and extending them to a broader reaction–diffusion setting, the paper offers a compact analytical framework for anomalous diffusion models arising in statistical physics, transport theory, complex media, and related applications.
outputs.L5:
### Caputo and Riesz Fractional Derivatives

This topic belongs to fractional calculus, a branch of mathematics that generalizes ordinary differentiation and integration to non-integer orders. Two important operators in this field are the **Caputo** and **Riesz** fractional derivatives.

The Caputo derivative is commonly used to describe time-dependent processes with memory. Its main advantage is that initial conditions can be expressed through standard integer-order derivatives, making it suitable for physical and engineering models. The Riesz derivative, in contrast, is generally associated with spatial processes. Because it is symmetric, it is often applied to anomalous diffusion, wave propagation, and systems involving long-range spatial interactions.

Equations combining Caputo time derivatives with Riesz space derivatives can model phenomena in which the present state depends on both past behavior and nonlocal spatial effects. This makes Caputo–Riesz models valuable in areas such as viscoelasticity, fluid dynamics, transport theory, and mathematical physics.

The model incorporates temporal memory, anomalous spatial transport, directional asymmetry, reaction effects, and external forcing within a single evolution equation. By applying Laplace and Fourier transforms, we derive an analytical representation of the solution for general initial data and source terms. The corresponding Green function is expressed in terms of Mittag–Leffler and Fox \(H\)-functions, providing a compact description of the underlying nonlocal dynamics. Fundamental properties of the solution, including scaling behavior, mass evolution, asymmetry, and limiting cases, are examined. The formulation recovers several classical and fractional diffusion, reaction–diffusion, and space–time transport models for appropriate choices of the derivative orders and skewness parameter. These results offer a versatile analytical basis for modeling anomalous transport processes in heterogeneous, memory-dependent, and spatially asymmetric media.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that solves a fractional reaction-diffusion equation using Laplace and Fourier transforms and expresses the closed-form solution in terms of the H-function.
counterfactuals.output:
The study develops an analytical solution for a generalized fractional reaction–diffusion equation, where the usual time derivative is replaced by a fractional derivative and the spatial operator may also allow anomalous diffusion. The equation includes reaction terms, diffusion coefficients, source functions, and prescribed initial conditions.

The solution procedure is:

1. **Laplace transform in time** converts the fractional time derivative into an algebraic expression involving the initial data.
2. **Fourier transform in space** converts the diffusion operator into a multiplication term in wave-number space.
3. The resulting algebraic equation is solved in the joint Laplace–Fourier domain.
4. Inverting the Laplace transform produces Mittag–Leffler-type functions.
5. The inverse Fourier transform is evaluated using Mellin-transform techniques, allowing the Green function and related solution kernels to be written compactly as **Fox \(H\)-functions**.

The final solution generally consists of a convolution of the \(H\)-function Green kernel with the initial condition, plus a space–time convolution with the source term. This representation is valuable because the Fox \(H\)-function unifies many familiar special functions and makes it possible to recover classical diffusion, time-fractional diffusion, space-fractional diffusion, and standard reaction–diffusion equations as limiting cases.

The study’s main contribution is therefore a broad closed-form framework for anomalous reaction–diffusion processes. The solution captures non-Gaussian spatial spreading and long-memory effects, while providing formulas suitable for deriving asymptotic behavior, moments, and special-case solutions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a scholarly paragraph explaining how the Riesz-Feller derivative provides a general framework encompassing space-time, neutral, space-fractional, and time-fractional diffusion models.
counterfactuals.output:
The Riesz–Feller derivative furnishes a unified spatial generator for a broad class of fractional diffusion equations through  
\[
{}^{C}D_t^{\beta}u(x,t)=\kappa\,{}_{x}D_{\theta}^{\alpha}u(x,t),
\qquad 0<\beta\le 1,\quad 0<\alpha\le 2,
\]
where its Fourier symbol, \(-|\xi|^{\alpha}e^{i\,\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)\theta\pi/2}\), encodes both the nonlocality of spatial transport through the order \(\alpha\) and its directional skewness through \(\theta\), subject to \(|\theta|\le \min\{\alpha,2-\alpha\}\). This space–time fractional equation contains several standard models as parameter regimes: \(\beta=1\) gives space-fractional diffusion generated by a possibly asymmetric stable Lévy process; \(\alpha=2\) and \(\theta=0\) yields time-fractional diffusion with the ordinary Laplacian; \(\alpha=\beta\) defines the neutral fractional diffusion model; and \(\alpha=2,\beta=1,\theta=0\) recovers classical Gaussian diffusion. Thus, by combining the Riesz–Feller spatial operator with a Caputo-type temporal derivative, one obtains a single analytic framework that continuously interpolates among space-fractional, time-fractional, neutral, and fully space–time fractional transport while retaining control over anomalous scaling and spatial asymmetry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise literature-oriented overview of generalized fractional reaction-diffusion equations, mentioning the earlier work of Mainardi et al. (2001, 2005) and Saxena et al. (2006a, b).
counterfactuals.output:
Generalized fractional reaction–diffusion equations replace the classical first-order time derivative and/or Laplacian by nonlocal operators, for example
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\,{}^{C}D_t^{\alpha_j}u(x,t)
=K\,D_{\theta}^{\beta}u(x,t)+R(u,x,t)+f(x,t),
\]
where \(0<\alpha_j\le 1\), \(D_{\theta}^{\beta}\) may be a Riesz or Riesz–Feller space-fractional derivative, and \(R\) denotes reaction, decay, or coupling. Such models describe anomalous transport with memory, heavy-tailed spatial jumps, and chemical or biological reactions; multi-term and distributed-order variants allow several relaxation scales.

The foundational analyses of Mainardi and collaborators (2001, 2005) developed the space–time fractional diffusion framework, emphasizing Fourier–Laplace methods, Green functions, scaling laws, and probabilistic interpretations. Their fundamental solutions were represented through Wright/M-Wright and Fox \(H\)-functions and linked to subordinated stochastic processes, providing the mathematical basis on which later reaction–diffusion extensions were built.

Saxena, Mathai, and Haubold (2006a, b) extended this transform-based approach to generalized fractional reaction–diffusion equations containing reaction terms, external sources, noninteger time derivatives, and Riesz–Feller spatial operators. They obtained explicit solutions for broad classes of initial-value problems in terms of Mittag–Leffler and Fox \(H\)-functions. These papers helped establish the now-standard solution strategy: Fourier transformation in space, Laplace transformation in time, algebraic resolution in transform space, and inversion through special-function identities.

Subsequent literature has expanded the theory to nonlinear reactions, coupled systems, variable coefficients, bounded domains, distributed-order derivatives, tempered operators, and numerical schemes. Central issues remain positivity and normalization of Green functions, well-posedness, asymptotic behavior, and the relation between fractional operators and underlying continuous-time random walks or subordination mechanisms.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a paper abstract describing the derivation and probabilistic interpretation of fundamental solutions to space-time fractional diffusion equations formulated with Caputo and Riesz-Feller derivatives.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract—** We derive the fundamental solutions of the Cauchy problem for space-time fractional diffusion equations in which temporal evolution is governed by a Caputo derivative of order \(0<\beta\leq 1\) and spatial transport by a Riesz–Feller derivative of order \(0<\alpha\leq 2\) and skewness \(\theta\), with \(|\theta|\leq \min\{\alpha,2-\alpha\}\). Applying Laplace and Fourier transforms yields the Green-function symbol
\[
\widetilde{\widehat{G}}_{\alpha,\beta}^{\theta}(k,s)
=\frac{s^{\beta-1}}{s^\beta+\kappa |k|^\alpha
e^{i\,\mathrm{sgn}(k)\theta\pi/2}},
\]
and hence the Fourier representation
\[
\widehat{G}_{\alpha,\beta}^{\theta}(k,t)
=E_\beta\!\left[-\kappa t^\beta |k|^\alpha
e^{i\,\mathrm{sgn}(k)\theta\pi/2}\right],
\]
where \(E_\beta\) is the Mittag–Leffler function. Mellin-transform and subordination arguments provide equivalent integral and special-function representations, together with the self-similar scaling \(G(x,t)=t^{-\beta/\alpha}G(xt^{-\beta/\alpha},1)\). Under the admissible parameter restrictions, the fundamental solution is nonnegative and normalized, and therefore defines a probability density. Probabilistically, it is the transition density of an asymmetric \(\alpha\)-stable Lévy motion evaluated at the inverse of an independent \(\beta\)-stable subordinator. This representation separates spatial jumps from temporal trapping and clarifies the roles of \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and \(\theta\) in anomalous spreading and skewness. Classical Gaussian diffusion, strictly stable Lévy motion, and time-fractional diffusion arise as limiting cases.
